content: 1. A treatment regimen extending for 8 months or longer is recommended in certain cases, but this recommendation is conditional and based on very low certainty in the available evidence. 2. In countries with high levels of isoniazid resistance, new tuberculosis (TB) patients with known or suspected resistance may receive a continuation phase therapy with HR (isoniazid and rifampicin) or HRE (isoniazid, rifampicin, and ethambutol) as an acceptable alternative. This is a conditional recommendation based on insufficient evidence and expert opinion. 3. For new pulmonary TB patients treated with a rifampicin-containing regimen, if a positive sputum smear is detected at the end of the intensive phase, extending the intensive phase is not recommended. This is a strong recommendation supported by high-quality evidence. 4. In cases of tuberculous meningitis, initial adjuvant corticosteroid therapy with dexamethasone or prednisolone tapered over 6–8 weeks is strongly recommended, supported by moderate certainty in the evidence. 5. For tuberculous pericarditis, initial adjuvant corticosteroid therapy may be used, but this is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty in the evidence. 6. For previously treated TB patients, specimens for culture and drug-susceptibility testing should be obtained before or at the start of treatment. Testing should include at least isoniazid and rifampicin. Rapid molecular-based drug-susceptibility testing results should guide the choice of regimen. 7. In settings where rapid molecular drug-susceptibility testing is available, the results should inform the selection of treatment regimens. 8. WHO is developing further guidance on the treatment of patients with isoniazid mono-resistance. 9. Health education and counseling on treatment adherence should be provided to all TB patients. This is a strong recommendation with moderate certainty in the evidence. 10. A package of treatment adherence interventions may be offered to TB patients alongside a suitable treatment administration option. This is a conditional recommendation with low certainty in the evidence. 11. Treatment adherence interventions, which may be complementary and not mutually exclusive, include: Tracer or digital medication monitoring (conditional recommendation, very low certainty). Material support to patients (conditional recommendation, moderate certainty). Psychological support to patients (conditional recommendation, low certainty). Education for healthcare staff (conditional recommendation, low certainty). 12. Community or home-based directly observed therapy (DOT) is recommended over health facility-based DOT or unsupervised treatment. This is a conditional recommendation with moderate certainty in the evidence. 13. DOT administered by trained lay providers or healthcare workers is recommended over DOT by family members or unsupervised treatment. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty in the evidence. 14. Video-observed treatment (VOT) can replace DOT when video communication technology is available and can be appropriately organized and operated by healthcare providers and patients. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty in the evidence. 15. A decentralized model of care is recommended over a centralized model for patients on multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) treatment. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty in the evidence. 16. Nutritional care and support for TB patients remain valid recommendations, with additional considerations for patient care and support. 17. Recommendations for managing childhood TB remain valid and should be read alongside accompanying remarks in relevant documents. 18. WHO guidelines for TB treatment are regularly updated to reflect new evidence and developments. The latest update aims to consolidate guidance for drug-susceptible and drug-resistant TB management into a single guideline. 19. The updated guidelines include evidence-based recommendations for TB treatment and patient care, focusing on areas where new evidence has emerged or where previous recommendations require revision. 20. The guidelines are intended for policymakers, national TB program managers, and healthcare professionals, including doctors, nurses, and educators, to inform country-specific TB treatment programs. 21. Recommendations are graded based on the certainty of evidence and the strength of the recommendation. Certainty levels range from high to very low, and recommendations may be strong or conditional depending on the balance of benefits, risks, and resource considerations. 22. Evidence for the guidelines was reviewed systematically, prioritizing randomized controlled trials and observational studies when trial data were limited. The GRADE methodology was used to assess the quality of evidence and develop recommendations. 23. The guidelines aim to provide clear, evidence-based recommendations while addressing the diverse needs of healthcare workers and patients in various settings.
